questions.question: A rural broadband provider is preparing a model that ranks incoming fault reports so engineers are dispatched to the most disruptive outages first. Its dispatch history is dense for town streets and thin for outlying farms, and the regulator has asked the provider to show that the ranking is fair. Which action addresses the fairness consideration for this solution?

options.A: Publish a notice on the customer portal explaining that the order of engineer dispatch is decided with the help of an AI system.
options.B: Compare how the model ranks town faults against outlying-farm faults of the same type, and report the gap between the two.
options.C: Encrypt the stored dispatch history and limit access to the ranking data to the operations team who run the dispatch desk.
options.D: Review a weekly sample of closed jobs to see whether any farm customers have complained about how long they waited.

rationale.correct: A fairness consideration asks where a solution could hand out attention or accuracy unevenly across groups of people, and the only way to answer it is to measure the outcome for each group. Ranking town faults beside outlying-farm faults of the same type turns the responsible AI question into a number the regulator can read.

distractors.A: Telling customers that an AI system orders dispatch discharges transparency. It describes the mechanism to people without revealing whether farms consistently wait longer than towns.
distractors.C: Encrypting the history and limiting access is a privacy and security control. It protects the data behind the ranking and says nothing about how the ranking treats each group.
distractors.D: Complaints surface only after people have already waited, and the customers who wait longest are often the least likely to complain, so the gap stays invisible.

questions.question: A ferry operator counts boarding passengers with a vision model so that no sailing exceeds its licensed capacity. The model was built on images captured in clear weather at the main terminal. On the exposed northern route, fog and spray leave the camera images washed out for part of the year. Which measure addresses the reliability and safety consideration here?

options.A: Retrain the counting model every quarter on the most recent boarding footage captured across all of the routes.
options.B: Display the counted figure on a screen at the gate with a note that the number is produced by an AI system.
options.C: Detect when image quality drops below what the model needs and hand the count to gate staff until it recovers.
options.D: Install a second camera at every gate so that more images of each boarding passenger reach the model.

rationale.correct: A reliability and safety consideration asks how the solution behaves when conditions fall outside what it was built for, and what catches it when they do. Fog and spray are exactly that condition, so the responsible AI answer is a detected quality floor with a manual fallback behind it, not a model that keeps counting through weather it cannot see.

distractors.A: A retraining cadence improves the model between refreshes and leaves every foggy sailing in the gap unprotected. The failure arrives with the weather, not with the calendar.
distractors.B: Showing the figure and its origin at the gate is a transparency measure. Passengers learn where the number came from and the vessel can still be loaded past its licensed capacity.
distractors.D: More cameras capture more of the same degraded images. Adding capture volume does not give the model a usable view when spray has washed the scene out.

questions.question: A dental practice group is building an assistant that answers clinicians' questions from the group's clinical notes. The clinical director is comfortable that the notes are held on the group's own systems and asks what else the privacy and security consideration requires before the assistant is opened to all sixteen practices. Which answer is correct?

options.A: Display a privacy statement in each waiting room describing how patient notes are used by the new assistant.
options.B: Give the assistant the notes from every practice so its answers stay consistent wherever a clinician asks.
options.C: Ask reception staff to strip patient names out of any note before they paste it into the assistant's window.
options.D: Scope which notes the assistant can reach for each role, and test whether crafted questions pull patient detail out of it.

rationale.correct: A privacy and security consideration asks what data the solution holds, who can reach it, and how it resists attempts to pull that data back out through the model itself. Role-scoped reach answers the second question and adversarial questioning answers the third, which is the part a responsible AI review of storage location never touches.

distractors.A: A waiting-room statement tells patients what happens to their notes. It is a transparency measure and it changes nothing about who can reach the notes through the assistant.
distractors.B: Handing every practice's notes to one assistant widens exposure to reach a consistency goal. Any single crafted question can now surface a patient from a practice the clinician never worked at.
distractors.C: Asking reception staff to redact by hand puts the control on the busiest people in the practice, and the notes the assistant already holds are untouched by anything typed into its window.

questions.question: A hearing-aid retail chain replaces its appointment line with a voice assistant that books fittings. In the pilot, callers with profound hearing loss and callers whose speech is affected by a stroke abandon the call far more often than other callers, and the chain has to decide what to do before the national rollout. Which action addresses the inclusiveness consideration?

options.A: Restrict the voice assistant to callers who have completed a short hearing questionnaire on the chain's website first.
options.B: Add a line to the booking page warning that the voice assistant may misunderstand some callers on the first attempt.
options.C: Test the assistant with callers who have hearing loss and affected speech, and add a text booking route where it fails.
options.D: Raise the microphone sensitivity of the voice assistant so that quieter and less distinct callers are picked up.

rationale.correct: An inclusiveness consideration asks whether the solution can actually be used by people across abilities and circumstances, not only by the callers it was convenient to build for. Testing with the affected callers is what turns that responsible AI question into evidence, and an alternative booking route is what makes the service usable for the people the voice path still fails.

distractors.A: Gating the assistant behind a website questionnaire removes the callers who struggle instead of serving them, and it assumes the same people can complete a web form unaided.
distractors.B: A warning on the booking page tells callers that they may not be understood. Being told about a barrier in advance does not get the appointment booked.
distractors.D: Microphone sensitivity is a capture setting. It changes what the audio picks up and does nothing for a caller whose speech the model cannot resolve into words.

questions.question: A charity's fundraising team launches a chat assistant that answers donor questions about how gifts are spent. Donors reach it from the donation page and many assume they are chatting to the supporter care team. Trustees ask what the transparency consideration obliges the charity to do. Which action is it?

options.A: Tell donors at the start of the chat that they are talking to an AI assistant and what it is not able to answer.
options.B: Keep a signed record of every answer the assistant gives so the board can hold a named trustee to account for it.
options.C: Publish the size of the model behind the assistant and the volume of text it was trained on in the annual report.
options.D: Have a fundraiser read a month of conversations and correct any answer that gave donors the wrong impression.

rationale.correct: A transparency consideration asks what users must be told about how the system works, what its limits are, and that they are dealing with an AI system at all. Donors who believe they reached supporter care have been told none of it, so the responsible AI obligation is discharged at the start of the conversation.

distractors.B: A signed record with a named owner is an accountability instrument. It settles who answers for a misleading reply and still leaves the donor believing they were talking to a person.
distractors.C: Model size and training volume are implementation figures. Donors cannot use either to understand what the assistant can and cannot tell them about their gift.
distractors.D: Reading a month of conversations afterwards catches misleading answers once donors have already acted on them, which is a detection step and not a disclosure.

questions.question: A coastal port authority ranks containers for physical inspection with a model, and inspectors work the ranked list from the top down. A mis-declared cargo passed through the port unopened, and the authority's board wants to know what the accountability consideration requires of the arrangement. Which answer is correct?

options.A: Have the model return a written explanation of the factors behind each container's position on the ranked list.
options.B: Name the officer who owns the inspection decision and set out the governance through which that decision is reviewed.
options.C: Log every ranking the model produced and every inspector response to it, so the record can be examined afterwards.
options.D: Move container ranking to a specialist cargo-risk supplier whose service already carries an assurance certificate.

rationale.correct: An accountability consideration asks who remains answerable for the outcome and through what governance, which is a different question from what the system is able to explain about itself. A responsible AI answer names the human owner of the inspection decision and the forum that reviews it, so the mis-declared cargo has somewhere to land.

distractors.A: An explanation of the ranking factors serves transparency. It helps an inspector understand the list and leaves the question of who answers for an unopened container unanswered.
distractors.C: A log preserves evidence for whoever eventually looks. It supports a review without creating the owner or the forum that would hold one.
distractors.D: Handing the ranking to a supplier moves the work outward. The port authority still admits the cargo, so the answerability it was asked about has not moved anywhere.

questions.question: A maritime insurer flags claims for manual review with a deployed model. Broker associations are pressing the insurer to publish the exact weight the model places on each factor so brokers can see why a claim was flagged. The insurer's fraud team says a broker holding those weights could shape a claim to sit just under the flag. Select TWO statements that correctly describe the obligations in play.

options.A: Telling brokers that a model flags claims, what it broadly weighs, and how to contest a flag discharges the transparency obligation.
options.B: Publishing the exact weights is required, as transparency outranks the other responsible AI considerations whenever they meet.
options.C: Withholding the exact weights serves the privacy and security consideration, which is the obligation pulling the other way here.
options.D: The conflict disappears once the insurer names a claims officer who is accountable for every flagged claim.
options.E: Raising the flagging threshold so fewer claims are flagged removes the need to explain the model's weights.

rationale.correct: One design decision can engage two responsible AI principles at once and they can pull in opposite directions. Here transparency obliges the insurer to tell brokers that a model flags claims, what it broadly weighs and how to contest a flag, while privacy and security is the obligation that argues for holding the exact weights back. Naming both is what the judgment consists of.

distractors.B: No responsible AI principle carries a standing rank over the others. Applying transparency as a rule that always wins is what hands the fraud team's objection away unexamined.
distractors.D: Naming an accountable claims officer discharges accountability. It settles who answers for a flag and leaves the question of what may be published exactly where it was.
distractors.E: Moving the threshold changes how many claims are flagged. The brokers whose claims are still flagged are owed the same explanation, so the obligation is untouched.

questions.question: An archival film restoration studio drafts catalog entries for restored reels with a deployed generative model. For one 1954 documentary the model wrote a fluent entry naming a director of photography who worked on no such film, and the studio's own records were never connected to the model. A restorer asks how that sentence came to exist. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: The model held a copy of its training material and returned the row that most closely matched the reel's title.
options.B: The model looked the credit up in a reference collection at request time and returned the nearest available match.
options.C: The model produced the entry one token at a time, picking each from patterns it learned during pre-training.
options.D: The model sorted the reel into a genre class and completed the credit fields from the typical values of that class.

rationale.correct: Large language models break input into tokens and produce output one token at a time, choosing each from patterns learned during pre-training and not from a stored record of anything they were shown. Tokenization and next-token selection are the whole mechanism, which is exactly why a fluent, specific and entirely unsupported credit can appear.

distractors.A: A generative model does not carry its training material as retrievable rows. Treating the output as a lookup makes the invented credit look like a data fault that could be corrected in a table.
distractors.B: Looking a fact up at request time describes a grounded solution connected to a source. This deployment had no such connection, so nothing was consulted when the entry was written.
distractors.D: Sorting an item into a class and filling fields from it describes a classification pipeline. The model was not classifying the reel; it was continuing text.

questions.question: A genealogy research service uses a deployed model to answer researchers' questions about transcribed parish registers. Two complaints recur: the model sometimes states a baptism date that appears in no register, and when a very long register is pasted in as one request, details from its opening pages stop showing up in the answers. Which explanation covers both complaints?

options.A: Both follow from how the model works: output is generated from learned patterns, and one request can only attend to a fixed amount of text.
options.B: Both indicate that the service has outgrown its model and needs one trained on a broader body of genealogical material.
options.C: The invented dates are transcription faults in the parish registers, and the missing detail is the request timing out part-way through the answer.
options.D: Both are effects of the sampling settings on the deployment and resolve once the temperature is turned down.

rationale.correct: Two limits follow directly from the mechanism behind Large language models: output can be fluent, specific and entirely unsupported, and there is a fixed amount of text the model can attend to in one request. A stated baptism date that no register holds is the first limit, and opening pages dropping out of a very long request is the second, so one explanation covers both prompts.

distractors.B: More training material would change what the model knows and neither limit is a knowledge gap. A broader model invents dates just as fluently and still attends to a fixed amount of text.
distractors.C: Transcription faults would put the wrong date in the register itself, and the answers stay complete rather than truncating, so nothing here points at a request that failed to finish.
distractors.D: Sampling settings move how varied the wording is. They do not create a record the model never had, and they do not extend how much text one request can attend to.

questions.question: A corporate travel management firm wants travelers to photograph a paper taxi receipt in the expense app and ask a question about it in the same step, such as whether the fare is claimable under their client's policy. The firm's platform team has to pick the model capability the feature needs before any code is written. Which one is it?

options.A: A chat and text generation model, with the traveler typing the fare and date from the receipt into the app first.
options.B: An embeddings model that turns the photographed receipt into a vector so the app can find similar past receipts.
options.C: An image generation model prompted with the policy wording so it renders the receipt in a readable format.
options.D: A multimodal model that takes the photograph and the traveler's typed question together in one request.

rationale.correct: Generative AI models are chosen by the capability the requirement needs, and this requirement puts an image and a question in the same request. A multimodal model is the capability class that accepts more than one input type, which is what lets the traveler photograph the receipt and ask about it in one step.

distractors.A: Text generation over typed values works only once the traveler has done the reading. It meets the requirement by moving the hard part of it onto the person holding the receipt.
distractors.B: Embeddings place content in a vector space for comparison. Finding similar receipts is a real capability of that model class and it answers no question about this client's policy.
distractors.C: Image generation produces new visual content from a description. Nothing in this requirement asks for a new image; the image already exists and has to be read.

questions.question: A craft brewery is putting its first generative feature into its trade-order portal and has picked a model in Microsoft Foundry. A developer tells the project group that deploying the model is simply switching it on, and that everything worth deciding is decided later in the client code. Which correction should the group hear?

options.A: Deployment only places the model files inside the project, and every meaningful choice is made by the calling application.
options.B: A deployment carries its own options for how the model is made available, and those options are settled when it is deployed.
options.C: Deployment settles nothing at all: the model's behavior comes entirely from the inference parameters sent on each request.
options.D: The choices belong to the model catalog, where the brewery compares the available models before picking one to work with.

rationale.correct: A model has to be deployed in Microsoft Foundry before anything can use it, and the deployment is not a single fixed act: it carries deployment options about how that model is made available. Treating it as an on switch hides decisions that are made at deployment time and are awkward to revisit once the portal is live.

distractors.A: A deployment is what makes a model callable, not a file drop. Describing it as storage leaves the project group expecting choices in the client code that were already made.
distractors.C: Inference parameters are real and they shape each response. They sit around a deployment that already exists and cannot make one available in the first place.
distractors.D: The model catalog is where a model is compared and chosen. It is a different surface from the deployment that publishes the chosen model for use.

questions.question: A cinema exhibition chain generates a short blurb for each film from the distributor's synopsis. Marketing needs the same synopsis to produce the same blurb every time it is regenerated, because the wording is printed on foyer cards and reused by twelve venues. Today the same request returns differently worded blurbs. Which change produces the behavior marketing asked for?

options.A: Lower the temperature on the requests so the model's token choices vary far less from one run to the next.
options.B: Raise the maximum output tokens on the requests so the model always has room to finish the blurb it started.
options.C: Move the house style rules into the system prompt so every request to the deployment carries the same wording rules.
options.D: Deploy a second copy of the model for marketing and cache the first blurb each film receives from the deployment.

rationale.correct: Inference behavior is governed by configuration parameters set around the deployment, and each parameter moves output in a stated direction. Repeatable wording for identical prompts is what a lower temperature produces, so the judgment is picking the parameter whose stated direction matches the behavior asked for.

distractors.B: The output length ceiling governs how much the model may produce. A longer allowance does not make two runs of the same request agree on their wording.
distractors.C: House style in the system prompt makes every blurb sound like the chain. Two runs under the same style rules still land on different sentences.
distractors.D: A second deployment with a cache in front of it freezes the first answer for each film and adds a copy of the model to run. The variation is still there the moment a blurb is regenerated.

questions.question: A waste collection services operator has five AI proposals from five different depots and wants each one named as an AI workload before any product or route is chosen. Match each proposal to the workload class it belongs to. Options may be used more than once.

scenarios.text: Depot supervisors dictate end-of-shift notes into a handset in the yard and need those notes available as text the same evening.
Weighbridge tickets arrive as scanned pages, and the finance system needs the tonnage, date and vehicle number from each ticket as named values.
Residents' complaint emails have to be routed by the service they mention, and the operations team wants the recurring terms across each month.
A camera on the lifting arm must flag a bin holding a gas cylinder before the load is tipped into the truck.
Residents who cannot read the printed collection calendar want the week's collection dates read out to them over the phone line.

rationale.correct: Naming the workload class is the decision that governs everything downstream, and it is decided by what goes in and what has to come out. Dictated notes turned into text and printed dates turned into audio are both speech work, which is why one class covers two of these proposals. Scanned tickets whose tonnage, date and vehicle number must arrive as named values are information extraction. Routing complaint emails by service and pulling out the terms that recur is text analysis. A camera judging what is inside a bin before it is tipped is computer vision.

questions.question: A bicycle-share operator already drafts nightly rebalancing plans with a deployed generative model: an analyst pastes in the docking telemetry and the model returns a written plan. The operations lead has been told the next step is agentic AI and assumes it means moving to a larger, better-writing model. Which statement corrects that assumption?

options.A: An agentic solution writes longer and better structured rebalancing plans than a model answering a single prompt.
options.B: An agentic solution is a model given a much larger context so that a whole night of docking telemetry fits in one request.
options.C: An agentic solution pursues the rebalancing goal across steps and acts on it, booking the van and issuing the move orders.
options.D: An agentic solution is a model fine-tuned on the operator's own history of overnight rebalancing decisions.

rationale.correct: Agentic AI is its own workload class and not a larger generative model. The distinguishing property of AI agents is that the solution pursues a goal across steps and takes actions, so booking the van and issuing the move orders is the change of class, while better prose is a change of degree.

distractors.A: Better written plans are a change in output quality within the same rung. The analyst still reads the plan and still does everything the plan describes.
distractors.B: A larger context lets one request hold more telemetry. The solution still answers and stops, which is the property that keeps it outside the agentic class.
distractors.D: Fine-tuning adapts a model to the operator's own style of plan. It changes what the model produces and never gives it a step to take.

questions.question: An independent bookstore chain collects several thousand customer reviews a month across its shops. The buying team does not want to read the reviews. It wants reviews that discuss the same thing to sit together in one index, and it wants to see month by month which subjects are rising across the shops. Which text analysis technique produces that?

options.A: Summarization of each review, so the buying team can read a condensed version of what every customer wrote.
options.B: Entity detection over each review, so the team receives the people, places and organizations that each one names.
options.C: Sentiment analysis of each review, so the team receives a polarity score showing how positive each customer was.
options.D: Keyword extraction over each review, so the team receives the salient terms that the review is actually about.

rationale.correct: Keyword extraction returns the salient terms a text is about, which is what a business wants when it needs to index, route or trend content instead of reading a condensed version of it. Grouping reviews that discuss the same thing and watching which subjects rise month by month are both built on those terms, so this is the text analysis output the requirement names.

distractors.A: Summarization returns shorter prose that preserves the substance of each review. It is still something to read, and thousands of short reads do not make an index.
distractors.B: Entity detection returns typed spans naming real things. Authors and shop names are useful and they are not the same as the subjects a review is about.
distractors.C: A polarity score says how the customer felt. It sorts reviews by mood without saying what any of them discussed.

questions.question: A heritage museum has already transcribed its donor correspondence, so the full text of every letter is held as text in the collections system. The collection holds a separate catalog record for each individual, each institution and each location it documents, and it files correspondence by year. Curators need every letter to surface which of those records it refers to, so the letter can be linked to each one. Which technique returns that?

options.A: Keyword extraction over each letter, returning the terms the letter is most about, ranked by how strongly they stand out.
options.B: Entity detection over each letter, returning typed spans for the people, places, organizations and dates it names.
options.C: Summarization of each letter, returning a short account of what the correspondent was writing to say.
options.D: Optical character recognition over each letter, returning the words on the page in the order they appear.

rationale.correct: Entity detection returns typed spans naming real things in the text, such as people, places, organizations, dates and quantities, which is a different output from a list of the terms that happen to be salient. Typed spans are what the collections system can match against catalog records, so this is the text analysis the linking work needs.

distractors.A: Salient terms describe what a letter is about. They arrive untyped, so nothing tells the collections system which of them is a person and which is a place.
distractors.C: A short account of the letter is prose for a curator to read. It carries no values the catalog can link against.
distractors.D: Reading characters off a page is the step that produced the transcripts the museum already holds. Running it again returns the same text and no typed values.

questions.question: A specialty coffee roasting subscription receives long written feedback from members. Most messages praise the roast and criticize the delivery in the same paragraph, and the current per-message score comes back neutral. The roastery wants to see how members feel about each thing they commented on. Which use of sentiment analysis meets that?

options.A: Sentiment analysis at the level of each aspect a member commented on, so roast and delivery carry their own polarity.
options.B: Sentiment analysis at the level of the whole message, with the resulting scores averaged across each week of feedback.
options.C: Keyword extraction over the feedback, returning the terms that members use most often when they write to the roastery.
options.D: A classification model trained on past feedback to sort each incoming message into a happy or an unhappy pile.

rationale.correct: Sentiment analysis returns polarity, and the granularity matters: one score for a whole document answers a different question from a score attached to each thing the writer commented on. A message praising the roast and criticizing the delivery only stops reading as neutral when the text analysis is done per aspect.

distractors.B: A document-level score is exactly what is coming back neutral today, and averaging those scores over a week hides the split even more thoroughly.
distractors.C: The terms members use are already fairly obvious to the roastery. Knowing that delivery is discussed says nothing about whether members are happy with it.
distractors.D: Sorting whole messages into two piles is a coarser version of the score that is already failing, and a mixed message has no correct pile.

questions.question: A vocational training college receives a long written placement report from every employer at the end of each term. The head of faculty has to act on what employers actually said before the next term is planned, and has no time to read the full set. Which text analysis technique fits what the head of faculty needs?

options.A: Keyword extraction across the reports, returning the terms that recur most often in what employers wrote.
options.B: Entity detection across the reports, returning the employers, qualifications and dates that each report names.
options.C: Summarization of each report, returning shorter prose that preserves the substance of what the employer said.
options.D: Sentiment analysis of each report, returning a polarity score for how positive the employer was about the placement.

rationale.correct: Summarization returns shorter prose that preserves the substance of the original, which is what a reader needs when the goal is to act on the content instead of cataloging what it mentions. The head of faculty has to plan a term from what employers said, and that is a reading task made shorter, not a set of tags.

distractors.A: Recurring terms show what employers kept mentioning. They do not carry the judgment an employer made about a placement, which is the part the planning turns on.
distractors.B: Typed spans for employers, qualifications and dates are catalog values. The head of faculty already knows who wrote and about what course.
distractors.D: A polarity score ranks the reports by mood. It shows where to look without saying what the employer actually asked the college to change.

questions.question: A driving school network asks instructors to record a spoken debrief in the car at the end of each lesson. Head office wants those debriefs held as searchable text in the pupil record, so that the existing text tools can index them and pull out the terms instructors keep raising. Which capability produces what head office needs?

options.A: Speech synthesis over the debriefs, so each pupil receives a spoken version of the instructor's comments.
options.B: A multimodal model that describes the driving scene recorded by the dashboard camera during each lesson.
options.C: Keyword extraction run over the recordings, returning the terms the instructor used during the spoken debrief.
options.D: Speech recognition over the debriefs, producing a transcript of each one that head office can then index.

rationale.correct: Speech recognition takes audio in and produces text out, so it is the capability a scenario needs whenever the useful artifact is a transcript that something else will then read. Head office wants indexing and term extraction over the debriefs, and both of those run on text that only speech work can produce from a recording.

distractors.A: Synthesis runs the other way, turning text into audio. It gives the pupil something to listen to and leaves head office with no text at all.
distractors.B: Describing the driving scene is vision work on a different input. The instructor's spoken judgment is the content head office asked about.
distractors.C: Extracting terms is the right ambition applied at the wrong point: a text technique has no input until the audio has been recognized.

questions.question: A national parks service publishes each trailhead's safety notice as text in its visitor app, where the wording is already held and edited. Visitors with low vision have asked to hear the notice for the trail they are standing at, on their own phone, without waiting for a ranger. Which capability delivers that?

options.A: Speech recognition in the app, so a ranger reading the notice aloud can be captured for the visitor to keep.
options.B: Speech synthesis in the app, so the stored wording of the notice is produced as audio the visitor can hear.
options.C: Optical character recognition in the app, so the words on the trailhead sign are returned to the visitor as text.
options.D: Translation of the notice in the app, so the visitor reads it on screen in whichever language they have set.

rationale.correct: Speech synthesis takes text in and produces audio out, so it is the capability a scenario needs whenever a person has to hear something instead of reading it. The parks service already holds the notice as text, which is the input this speech capability consumes.

distractors.A: Recognition turns audio into text. It needs a ranger to speak first, which is the wait the visitors asked to avoid, and it produces something to read.
distractors.C: Reading the characters off the physical sign produces text the service already holds and edits, so the step returns the visitor to where they started.
distractors.D: Translation changes the language of the notice on the screen. A visitor who cannot read the screen is no better served in any language.

questions.question: A quarry wants one camera feed over its loading bay to do two things: confirm which product each haul truck is carrying, and count how many trucks are waiting in the bay at any moment. A single overall description of the scene has already been trialed and did not support either job. Select TWO outputs the vision work has to produce.

options.A: A caption describing what is happening in the loading bay at the moment the frame was taken.
options.B: A label for the product visible in the bed of a truck in the frame.
options.C: A generated image of a correctly loaded truck for the bay operator to compare against.
options.D: A timestamp written into each frame of the recorded loading-bay footage.
options.E: Located instances of each truck within the frame, so the waiting trucks can be counted.

rationale.correct: What a vision model can be asked to report about an image differs by granularity, and the business need picks the granularity. Computer vision tasks and techniques here split cleanly: confirming the product carried is a label for what is in the frame, and counting waiting trucks needs each truck located as its own instance. One requirement therefore buys two different outputs.

distractors.A: A description of the scene is the granularity that was already trialed. It reads well and it neither names the product reliably nor separates one truck from another.
distractors.C: Producing a reference image is generation rather than analysis. It gives the operator something to look at and reports nothing about the trucks in the bay.
distractors.D: A frame timestamp is a recording detail. It helps someone find the footage later and answers neither of the two questions the quarry asked.

questions.question: A fashion resale platform is preparing a seasonal campaign for garment styles it has not yet taken in stock, so no seller photographs of them exist. The marketing team wants studio-style visuals produced from written descriptions of each style. Which capability class does that campaign work need?

options.A: An image analysis call over the platform's existing seller photographs, describing what each garment in them is.
options.B: An optical character recognition call over the seller photographs, reading the brand and size from the garment labels.
options.C: An image generation model, producing new visuals from the written description of each garment style.
options.D: A model fine-tuned on the platform's own photographs so that searches return closer visual matches to a style.

rationale.correct: Image generation is a separate capability class from image analysis, and the two sit on opposite sides of computer vision: image-generation models produce new visual content from a description, while analysis reports on visual content that already exists. The campaign needs visuals of garments the platform has never held, so nothing existing can be reported on and only the generative class can serve it.

distractors.A: Describing existing seller photographs reports on stock the platform already has. The campaign is about styles it has not taken in, so there is nothing to describe.
distractors.B: Reading labels off photographs returns text from images that exist. It is useful cataloging work and produces no campaign visual.
distractors.D: Fine-tuning for closer visual matches improves retrieval over the existing library. Better search still cannot surface a photograph that was never taken.

questions.question: A household moving services company is consolidating five separate backlogs into one information extraction project, and the project lead has to state the content type each backlog presents before any extraction is configured. Match each backlog to its content type. Options may be used more than once.

scenarios.text: Photographs taken by crews on arrival showing damage to furniture before it is loaded.
Recordings from the booking line on which customers state their address, dates and access restrictions.
Quotation requests typed by customers into the website form and stored as they were written.
Dashcam footage of the approach to each property, kept for disputes about access and parking.
Photographs of the labels on packed crates showing the room and the destination address.

rationale.correct: Information extraction is one workload that spans four content types, so recognizing which type a backlog actually presents is the first decision and not an implementation detail. Damage photographs and crate-label photographs are both images, which is why one content type covers two of these backlogs. Booking-line recordings are audio, typed quotation requests are text, and dashcam footage of the approach is video. Naming the type is what tells the project lead which extraction path each backlog takes.

questions.question: A customs brokerage receives commercial invoices from shippers as scanned pages in dozens of house layouts, and a handful of new shippers onboard every month. Every declaration it files needs the same details lifted off the invoice and handed to the declaration system ready to post, with no clerk reading the page and no parsing code written per layout. Which technique meets that requirement?

options.A: Character reading over each scan, returning the words and figures of the page in the order they appear on it.
options.B: Keyword extraction over each scanned invoice, returning the terms that the invoice is most about.
options.C: A position template configured once per shipper layout, so each field is read from a fixed place on the scanned page.
options.D: Field extraction over each scan, returning invoice number, currency, total and consignee as named values.

rationale.correct: Reading the characters off content is not the same as extracting fields from it. Optical character recognition (OCR) returns text in the order it appears, while Field extraction and mapping returns named values a downstream system can use without further parsing. The declaration system needs values it can post, so only the field-level output removes both the clerk and the per-layout parsing code.

distractors.A: Page text in reading order is exactly the output that forces parsing code per house layout, which is the work the brokerage asked to remove.
distractors.B: Salient terms describe what an invoice is about. A declaration needs the consignee and the total, not the subject matter of the document.
distractors.C: A template does lift the fields off the page without a clerk, and it does it by fixing where each field sits. Dozens of house layouts means dozens of templates, and every new shipper needs another, so the per-layout work moves from code to configuration rather than going away.

questions.question: A postal sorting operation runs an assistant that answers staff questions about handling rules. Today every question is sent with a long block of text setting out the assistant's role, its tone and what it must never advise on. When a busy operator forgets to paste that block, the assistant answers in marketing tone and volunteers guidance on opening damaged items. Which change fixes this properly?

options.A: Keep the block where it is and have the client application paste it in front of every question an operator types.
options.B: Fine-tune the deployment on past answers so the role and tone are learned and no instruction text is needed at all.
options.C: Move the role, tone and prohibitions into the system prompt and leave the operator's question as the user prompt.
options.D: Lower the temperature on the deployment so the assistant stops volunteering guidance nobody asked it for.

rationale.correct: Standing behavior — persona, boundaries and rules that must hold on every turn — belongs in the system prompt, while the user prompt carries the request that changes from turn to turn. Splitting them that way means an operator cannot omit the rules, because the rules are no longer part of what an operator types.

distractors.A: Pasting the block automatically hides the symptom in one client. The rules still travel as part of each request, so any other caller can drop them again.
distractors.B: Fine-tuning teaches a style and cannot express a hard prohibition that has to hold on every turn. It is also a heavy answer to a placement problem.
distractors.D: Temperature governs how varied the wording is. A steadier voice offering the same prohibited guidance is not the correction this needs.

questions.question: A laboratory instrument servicing firm turns engineers' free-text visit notes into service records with a deployed model. The model reliably picks out the right facts — instrument, fault, parts fitted, calibration result — but writes them as flowing paragraphs, while the maintenance system needs a fixed layout with each field on its own line and units appended. Which correction fits the failure?

options.A: Put two or three worked examples of a finished service record into the prompt, so that the exact layout wanted is shown.
options.B: Ask the model to work through its reasoning step by step before it writes the service record out.
options.C: Fine-tune a copy of the model on several thousand past service records taken from the maintenance system.
options.D: Ask the engineers to write their visit notes in the required field-per-line layout so the model can copy that shape through.

rationale.correct: Worked examples inside the user prompt are the low-effort correction when the model understands the task but returns the wrong shape, format or register of answer. The facts are already right here, so the prompts need to show the layout wanted instead of describing it.

distractors.B: Step-by-step reasoning helps a task that breaks down partway through a chain of steps. Nothing in this task is going wrong on the way to the answer.
distractors.C: Fine-tuning on thousands of records is a heavy way to fix a layout, and it commits the firm to retraining whenever the maintenance system changes a field.
distractors.D: Asking engineers to write in the target layout moves the work back onto the people the tool exists to help, and free-text notes are the input the firm actually has.

questions.question: A shipping container leasing firm has a deployed model compute off-hire settlements: apply the daily rate for the hire period, subtract the free days, add damage charges, then apply the customer's discount band. The layout of the answer is always right, and the figure is often wrong — most commonly the discount has been applied before the damage charges. Which correction fits this failure?

options.A: Add three worked examples of finished settlements to the prompt so the model can see the shape of a good answer.
options.B: Raise the maximum output tokens so the model has room to complete the whole settlement in one response.
options.C: Split the settlement into four separate requests, one per rule, and have the client application add up the results.
options.D: Ask the model to work through the settlement step by step in the stated order before it gives the final figure.

rationale.correct: Asking the model to work through its reasoning step by step is the correction for a task that fails partway through a multi-step chain, which is a different failure from returning the wrong format. The layout is already correct and the order of operations is what slips, so the prompts have to make that order explicit work.

distractors.A: Worked examples correct the shape of an answer. The shape here is already right, and an example of a correct total does not stop the next settlement from applying the discount early.
distractors.B: A longer output allowance would matter if answers were being cut short. These answers finish; they finish with the wrong number.
distractors.C: Four requests plus client-side arithmetic rebuilds the calculation outside the model and adds moving parts to maintain for a fault that lives in the ordering.

questions.question: An orchard cooperative's developer has chosen a chat model from the catalog in the Foundry portal, written the grading-advice client and configured it with the project's address and credentials. Every call comes back saying the model cannot be found, and the project itself is reachable. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: The chosen model has to be added to the project as a connection before any client can reach the catalog entry.
options.B: The chosen model has not been deployed, and a model can only be called once a deployment of it exists.
options.C: The chosen model has to be exercised in the portal playground first, which is what enables calls from code.
options.D: The project needs a larger quota before a model of that size will accept requests from outside the portal.

rationale.correct: A model has to be deployed in the Foundry portal before anything can interact with it, so a scenario where nobody can call the model yet is a deployment step that has not happened. Choosing a model from the catalog records an intention; the deployment is what publishes it for use.

distractors.A: Connections attach external resources to a project. They are a real part of the portal and none of them turns a catalog listing into something callable.
distractors.C: The playground is a place to try a model that has already been deployed. Using it is optional and it grants nothing to code.
distractors.D: Quota governs how much traffic a live deployment may take. A model that was never deployed has no traffic to limit.

questions.question: A district heating utility ran its fault-triage pilot inside the portal, and engineers are happy with the answers. The utility now wants its field-service mobile app, which runs outside the portal on the engineers' handsets, to use the same deployed model. What does the app have to be pointed at?

options.A: The endpoint the deployment exposes, configured in the app with that endpoint's address and credentials.
options.B: The catalog entry for the chosen model, which the app queries by model name whenever an engineer asks.
options.C: A copy of the model files downloaded into the app so each handset answers without a network round trip.
options.D: Nothing further: an app owned by the same subscription reaches a deployment automatically once it exists.

rationale.correct: Anything deployed in Foundry is reached through an endpoint, and Microsoft Foundry endpoints are what an application outside the portal actually talks to. Pointing the field-service app at the deployment's endpoint and configuring its credentials is the step that turns a portal pilot into something the handsets can use.

distractors.B: The catalog is where models are compared and chosen. It lists what could be deployed and serves no traffic from an application.
distractors.C: Running the model on the handset is a different delivery model altogether and is not what a Foundry deployment provides.
distractors.D: Sharing a subscription grants no automatic route. Without a configured endpoint the app has no address to send a request to.

questions.question: A glass manufacturer's production manager wants to know whether a model can make sense of the plant's shift handover notes, which are terse and full of local abbreviations, before asking for budget. There is no application yet and no developer free for three weeks. Which route answers the question soonest without prejudging it?

options.A: Wait three weeks for a developer to become free, then have a small client written against the deployment with the Foundry SDK.
options.B: Commission a fine-tune on two years of handover notes so the model is judged on plant vocabulary.
options.C: Try the deployed model interactively in the Foundry portal, pasting in real handover notes and reading what comes back.
options.D: Ask the shift supervisors whether they believe a model could make sense of the way they write handovers.

rationale.correct: The Foundry portal offers a place to try a deployed model interactively before any application exists, which is the right route when the question is whether the model can do the job at all. Real handover notes pasted in produce the evidence the budget conversation needs, and nothing has to be built to get it.

distractors.A: Waiting three weeks postpones a question that can be answered today, and it spends developer time before anyone knows whether the answer is yes.
distractors.B: A fine-tune is a commitment made before the basic question has been answered, and two years of notes cost real effort to prepare.
distractors.D: Supervisors' expectations are informed opinion about their own writing. They are not a test of what the model does with it.

questions.question: A horticulture nursery has a model deployed and has confirmed in the portal that it answers growers' pest-treatment questions well. The nursery now wants growers to ask those questions from inside the stock app they already use on the packing line, without opening a browser. What does that step involve?

options.A: Exporting the tested Foundry portal conversation and embedding it in the stock app as a saved script of answers.
options.B: Writing code with the Foundry SDK that connects to the deployment, sends the prompts and handles the responses.
options.C: Deploying a second copy of the model for the stock app so that portal testing and packing-line traffic stay apart.
options.D: Adding every grower as a user of the portal so they can chat with the deployed model from the packing line.

rationale.correct: The Foundry SDK is what turns a deployed model into part of an application: a lightweight chat client application is code that connects to the deployment, sends the prompts and handles what comes back. That code is the whole of the step between a model that works in the portal and one growers can use where they work.

distractors.A: A portal conversation is a transcript of one session. Replaying saved answers cannot respond to a question a grower has not asked before.
distractors.C: A second deployment separates traffic and writes none of the code the stock app needs, so the growers are no closer to asking anything.
distractors.D: Giving growers portal access sends them to a browser and an authoring surface, which is precisely what the nursery asked to avoid.

questions.question: An electronics repair franchise is building a single-agent solution in the portal to help branch staff diagnose faults and order parts. The project plan lists writing the agent's instructions and connecting its tools, then marks the build complete and hands the agent to the branches. Select TWO statements that correct the plan.

options.A: Testing the agent in the portal is part of creating it, not a separate exercise the branches take on afterward.
options.B: An agent that has instructions and connected tools is finished, and any remaining checks belong to the branches.
options.C: Testing can be satisfied by having the author of the agent's instructions read them through once more.
options.D: The agent has to be exercised in the portal against the kind of requests branch staff will really send.
options.E: Testing here means measuring how quickly the agent's tool calls return inside the portal session.

rationale.correct: Creating a single-agent solution in the portal includes testing it there, so a plan that treats the agent as finished once it is defined has skipped a step the task itself names. To create and test means exercising the agent against realistic branch requests before anyone in a branch depends on it.

distractors.B: Declaring the build complete at definition hands an untested agent to the people least able to judge it, and it postpones the step that would have found the problems.
distractors.C: A re-read by the person who wrote the instructions is anchored to the assumptions that produced them, so it cannot see what those assumptions missed.
distractors.E: Tool-call timings describe how quickly the agent responds. Speed is worth knowing and says nothing about whether the diagnosis was right.

keywords: lightweight client application for an agent
questions.question: A wine estate has created and tested an agent in the portal that answers cellar-door questions, checks tasting availability and books slots through its connected tools. The estate already has a small chat client that talks to a bare model deployment, and the team proposes reusing that client unchanged to reach the agent. Which response is correct?

options.A: Reuse it unchanged: any client that can send a prompt to a deployment drives an agent in the same way.
options.B: Reuse it and paste the agent's instructions and tool descriptions into every request the client sends.
options.C: Keep staff working in the Foundry portal, as an agent cannot be reached from an application the estate writes with the Foundry SDK.
options.D: Write a client for the agent with the Foundry SDK, addressing the agent that already carries its instructions and tools.

rationale.correct: An agent gets its own lightweight client application for an agent, which is not the same code as a chat client over a bare model: the agent already carries the instructions, tools and state the chat client would otherwise have had to supply on every request. The Foundry SDK is what that client is written with.

distractors.A: A bare-model client and an agent client address different things. Treating them as interchangeable leaves the estate wondering why its tools are never called.
distractors.B: Pasting instructions and tool descriptions into each request pushes the agent back down to a model answering from a prompt, and the booking tool still never runs.
distractors.C: Staying in the portal abandons the cellar-door integration the estate asked for, and an agent is reachable from an application the estate writes.

questions.question: A sports stadium operations team has four AI requests to fund this quarter and has to pick the rung each one needs: over-reaching costs more to build and run, and under-reaching cannot meet the requirement. Match each request to the rung it needs. Options may be used more than once.
matching_options: A model answering from a prompt

scenarios.text: Marketing wants first drafts of matchday social posts written from a set of match facts that a person pastes in.
Stewards want to ask in plain language for current turnstile counts, with the answer pulled from the ticketing and access systems.
Hospitality wants a request such as moving a suite booking to check availability, change the booking and send the confirmation with nobody stepping in between.
A concert changeover request should be planned by separate staffing, transport and catering specialists working their own parts and reporting into a coordinator.

answer.s1: A model answering from a prompt

rationale.correct: The same platform builds several different things, and the requirement picks the rung. Drafting posts from facts a person supplies needs nothing beyond a model answering from a prompt. Reading live turnstile counts out of the ticketing and access systems needs AI agents that call tools, and so does changing a suite booking and sending the confirmation, which is why one rung covers two of these requests as a single-agent solution each. Only the changeover, where separate specialists plan their own parts and report into a coordinator, justifies several agents coordinated — the point at which agentic AI stops being one agent's work.

questions.question: A geothermal energy operator's agent answers drilling-procedure questions for well-site crews. Reviewers find the answers are sound general industry practice but do not follow the operator's own approved procedures, and a crew supervisor cannot tell which procedure any answer came from. Which change addresses both findings?

options.A: Connect the agent to a knowledge base built from the approved procedures, so answers draw on them and cite them.
options.B: Add a line to the agent's instructions telling it to answer only from the operator's approved procedures.
options.C: Fine-tune the model behind the agent on the operator's library of approved drilling procedures.
options.D: Have a senior drilling engineer check each answer against the approved procedures before a crew acts on it.

rationale.correct: An agent is grounded in an organization's own content by connecting it to a knowledge base, so its answers are drawn from approved material and carry citations back to it. Knowledge bases are what make grounded, citation-backed responses possible, which is what lets a supervisor see which procedure an answer rests on.

distractors.B: An instruction states the intent at the prompt layer while leaving the agent with no approved procedure to read, so it keeps answering from general practice.
distractors.C: Fine-tuning shapes how the model writes and leaves no trace a supervisor can follow back to a numbered procedure.
distractors.D: Expert review catches wrong answers one at a time after they are written, and it makes the crew wait for the reviewer every time.

questions.question: An inland waterway freight operator has an assistant that answers crews' navigation-rule questions from the operator's own rulebook. A review of a month of answers finds them clear, confident and well written, and finds that a small share of them state a bridge clearance limit that appears nowhere in the rulebook, with nothing in the answer showing where it came from. Which reading of this review is correct?

options.A: The answers are acceptable while they read clearly, as fluency is what crews actually judge an assistant on when they are under way.
options.B: A fluent answer is not a grounded answer, and one that cannot be traced to the rulebook is the failure grounding prevents.
options.C: The invented limits will fall away once crews are trained to ask the assistant more precisely worded questions.
options.D: Lowering the temperature on the deployment will stop the assistant stating limits the rulebook does not contain.

rationale.correct: A grounded answer and a fluent answer are different things: output that reads well but cannot be traced back to the content it was supposed to draw on is exactly the failure grounding exists to prevent. The review's own finding — a clearance limit in no rulebook, with nothing to trace it to — is the case for grounded, citation-backed responses.

distractors.A: Confidence is the property that makes an unsupported clearance limit dangerous on a bridge approach, so fluency cannot be the standard the answers are judged against.
distractors.C: Better-worded questions ask crews to work around the assistant, and a well-worded question can be answered with an invented limit just as fluently.
distractors.D: Temperature governs how varied the wording is. Steadier phrasing of an unsupported limit leaves the crew with the same untraceable number.

keywords: lightweight application that includes text analysis
questions.question: A veterinary hospital group is building an application over incoming referral letters. It has to route each letter by the service the referring vet is asking for, flag letters where the vet has expressed concern about waiting time, and link the practices named in the letter to records. A developer proposes one call per letter asking a general model to handle all of it. What does building this application actually involve?

options.A: One call per letter with the whole job described in the prompt, and the routing, the flag and the links read out of the reply text.
options.B: One deployment per requirement, with every letter routed through all three deployments in turn.
options.C: Choosing which technique the application calls for each stage of the work, then handling the structured result each returns.
options.D: Extracting the fields from each letter first, then deciding which technique to run based on what came back.

rationale.correct: Building a lightweight application that includes text analysis means picking which technique the application actually calls for each stage of the work, then handling the structured result it returns. Routing, flagging concern and linking named practices are three different asks, and each has a technique whose output the application can act on.

distractors.A: One prose reply that has to be read apart by the application removes the structure the application depends on, and it merges three asks into one instruction.
distractors.B: A deployment per requirement adds machinery the work does not need. The requirement is a choice of technique, not a fleet of models.
distractors.D: Deciding the technique after extracting fields inverts the order: the technique is what produces the structured result in the first place.

questions.question: A school district already runs an agent that answers staff questions and raises tickets through its connected tools. The district now wants parent messages classified by topic and by how upset the writer sounds, so the agent can prioritize what it raises. A developer proposes doing that classification in the mail gateway and passing only the result to the agent. Which design fits what the district asked for?

options.A: Classify in the mail gateway before the agent is involved, and pass the topic and the tone through to the agent as fields.
options.B: Describe in the agent's instructions how to judge topic and tone, so it forms both judgments as it reads.
options.C: Stand up a second agent whose only job is classification and have the two agents exchange messages.
options.D: Attach Azure Language text analysis to the agent as a capability it calls when a message needs classifying.

rationale.correct: Text analysis can be attached to an agent as a capability the agent uses when it needs it, instead of being a separate service the application calls before the agent ever runs. Attaching Azure Language to the agent keeps the judgment inside the agent's own work, which is what lets AI agents decide what to raise and in what order.

distractors.A: Classifying in the gateway fixes the order in advance and runs on every message whether the agent needs the judgment or not.
distractors.B: Instructions can describe how to judge tone, and doing so drops a dedicated capability in favor of prose the agent has to reinterpret each time.
distractors.C: A second agent to classify messages is a coordination problem invented to avoid attaching a capability to the agent that already exists.

questions.question: An aged-care operator has bedside devices on which residents speak requests such as asking what is for lunch or to have a nurse called. The current design records the audio, sends it to a recognition step, and sends the resulting text on to a model. The team wants to respond to spoken prompts with a deployed multimodal model instead. What changes?

options.A: The recognition step stays in front, and the multimodal model reads the transcript it produces.
options.B: The audio goes to the deployed multimodal model itself, so no separate recognition step sits in front of it.
options.C: The multimodal model has to be fine-tuned on recordings of residents before it will accept audio at all.
options.D: Multimodal describes the model speaking its answers as well as writing them, while its input stays text.

rationale.correct: A deployed multimodal model can respond to spoken prompts directly, which means the audio goes to the model itself instead of through a separate transcription step first. Removing that step is the whole change: one request carries the resident's spoken words to the model that answers them.

distractors.A: Keeping recognition in front describes the design the operator already has. The transcription step is exactly what the change removes.
distractors.C: Fine-tuning adapts a model to particular material and is not what makes a multimodal model able to take audio in.
distractors.D: Accepting more than one input type is the property in question here. Reading the term as an output style leaves the recording pipeline in place.

questions.question: A mobile network operator runs an incident bridge on which engineers speak status updates and hear updates read back to them. The application has to take dictated updates as text and read the consolidated status out in one consistent voice across every region. How is that speech work implemented on this platform?

options.A: Azure Speech in Foundry Tools provides Speech recognition and Speech synthesis as capabilities the application configures and calls.
options.B: A chat model deployed in Microsoft Foundry is prompted to transcribe each update and to write the consolidated status in a speaking style.
options.C: Speech behavior is set through the deployment's inference parameters, alongside settings such as temperature.
options.D: The portal playground carries out the recognition and the speaking for applications while they are running.

rationale.correct: Azure Speech in Foundry Tools is the dedicated route for speech work, implementing recognition and synthesis as capabilities an application configures and calls instead of behavior prompted out of a model. A consistent voice across regions is a configuration the application sets, which is what this route gives it.

distractors.B: A chat model prompted to transcribe is a general capability aimed at a job the platform already performs directly, and nothing in it produces audio to hear.
distractors.C: Inference parameters shape a model's text output. They sit around a model deployment and configure no speech capability.
distractors.D: The playground is a place for a person to try things interactively. It is not a component a running application calls.

questions.question: A rail freight terminal is adding spoken interaction to its yard app: shunters speak instructions over a noisy radio channel and hear confirmations read back. Both supported routes are open to the terminal, and it must decide between Azure Speech in Foundry Tools and a deployed multimodal model. Select TWO requirements that point to the dedicated speech capability.

options.A: The terminal wants one deployment to carry both the spoken exchange and its reasoning about the yard plan.
options.B: The terminal would rather configure the route in a portal than write and maintain prompts for it.
options.C: The confirmation voice has to sound identical on every yard radio, under the terminal's own control.
options.D: The terminal expects to add image checks of wagon seals to the same exchange later in the year.
options.E: Recognition has to be tuned to the yard's shunting vocabulary and answer within a predictable time.

rationale.correct: Speech has two supported routes on this platform, and a stated constraint decides between them. Control over how the voice sounds and recognition tuned to a specific vocabulary with predictable latency are what Azure Speech in Foundry Tools is configured and called for, so both of those requirements point away from prompting a general model.

distractors.A: Carrying the exchange and the reasoning in one deployment is a real constraint and it argues the other way, toward the multimodal model route.
distractors.B: A preference for portal configuration describes how the team likes to work. It is not a property of the spoken interaction the yard needs.
distractors.D: Adding image checks to the same exchange is about how many input types one route must accept, which again favors the multimodal model.

questions.question: A zoological park has an agent that books veterinary slots and logs feeding records through its connected tools. Keepers work with both hands occupied and want to speak their requests to that agent and hear its answers, without stopping to type. How is that built?

options.A: Replace the agent with Azure Speech in Foundry Tools, which recognizes the keeper's request and speaks a reply straight back.
options.B: Add recognition in front of the agent and have keepers read the agent's answer from the handset screen.
options.C: Instruct the agent to phrase its answers so that they sound natural when a keeper reads them aloud.
options.D: Compose Speech recognition and Speech synthesis around the agent, so that speech reaches it and its answer returns as audio.

rationale.correct: Creating a speech-capable agent means composing recognition and synthesis around an agent, so that a spoken request reaches the agent's reasoning and the agent's answer comes back as audio. The agent keeps its tools and its judgment; speech is wrapped around it at both ends.

distractors.A: A speech capability on its own hears and speaks and books nothing. Dropping the agent takes the tools and the reasoning out of the solution.
distractors.B: Recognition alone solves half the problem and leaves keepers reading a screen, which is the position their occupied hands put them in already.
distractors.C: Answers written to be read aloud still have to be read by somebody. The wording changes and no audio is produced.

questions.question: A textile manufacturer processes tens of thousands of short supplier messages a month, needing a polarity score and the key terms from each. A trial that prompts a general-purpose model returns good results, and the trial also shows per-message cost and response time above what the ordering system can absorb, with the reply shape varying enough to break the parser twice a week. Which route fits the requirement?

options.A: Keep the general-purpose model and shorten the prompt so that each message costs less to process.
options.B: Keep the general-purpose model and run the messages overnight in one batch to spread the cost out.
options.C: Use the purpose-built text analysis capability, which performs this task at lower cost in a consistent shape.
options.D: Fine-tune a general-purpose model on past supplier messages so it answers the same task more cheaply.

rationale.correct: Inside a capability there is a build-or-buy decision, and a purpose-built capability that already performs the task can beat prompting a general-purpose model when cost, latency or consistency dominate the requirement. All three dominate here, which is what settles it against Generative AI models for this stage of the work.

distractors.A: A shorter prompt trims part of the per-message cost and leaves the response time and the varying reply shape exactly where they are.
distractors.B: Batching overnight moves when the work happens. The ordering system needs the scores as messages arrive, so the delay is the requirement being dropped.
distractors.D: Fine-tuning adapts a model to the manufacturer's material and does not make a general-purpose model cheaper per message to call.

keywords: lightweight application that includes text analysis
questions.question: A water testing laboratory takes sample results by phone from field samplers. Every call is to be classified by the contaminant the sampler names and flagged when the sampler states a reading outside the expected range, and the laboratory has chosen Azure Language text analysis to do both. A design document shows the classification step reading the call audio, with a transcript produced afterward for the archive. Which correction does the design need?

options.A: Recognition has to run first, and only then can a text technique be applied to its output.
options.B: Both steps can run against the audio at once, with their two results joined before the record is written.
options.C: The archive transcript is optional, because the text step is able to work from the recorded call directly.
options.D: The order is immaterial as long as both steps have finished before the record reaches the archive.

rationale.correct: A voice workload runs in a fixed order: the audio is turned into text first, and only then can any text technique be applied to it. A lightweight application that includes text analysis over recorded calls has no input at all until speech recognition has produced one, so a design that classifies before it recognizes is classifying nothing.

distractors.B: Running both at once assumes the classifier has an input while the audio is still audio. There is nothing for it to read until recognition finishes.
distractors.C: Treating the transcript as optional leaves a text analysis service with nothing to read: the chosen route takes text, not audio, so the archive copy is the load-bearing part of the design.
distractors.D: Order is the whole constraint here. Two steps that both finish in the wrong sequence still produce a classification with no text behind it.

questions.question: A building inspection firm sends surveyors out with a tablet. A surveyor photographs a wall defect and needs a written opinion, phrased for the inspection report, on whether the pattern looks more like water ingress or settlement cracking. Which implementation produces that?

options.A: Send the photograph to an image generation model together with the report wording as its prompt.
options.B: Supply the photograph inside the prompt to a deployed multimodal model and ask the question the report needs.
options.C: Run character reading over the photograph and describe the defect from whatever text is found on the wall.
options.D: Have the surveyor describe the defect in words on the tablet and send only that description to the model.

rationale.correct: Visual input can be supplied inside a prompt to a deployed multimodal model, and what comes back is a natural-language answer about the image shaped by what the prompt asked for. Interpret visual input in prompts is exactly this shape of work: the photograph and the surveyor's question travel together, and the answer arrives in the register the report needs.

distractors.A: An image generation model produces pictures from descriptions. Sending it a photograph and a report style yields another image and no opinion.
distractors.C: Reading characters returns any text printed on the surface. A crack carries no writing, so this returns nothing about the defect.
distractors.D: A written description sends the model the surveyor's own judgment. The photograph, which is the evidence in question, never reaches the model.

questions.question: A printing and packaging firm's design studio has one deployed multimodal model that its app uses to read photographs of finished cartons for quality notes. A client has now asked for concept visuals of carton designs that have never been produced, worked up from a written brief. What does the app have to call for this new work?

options.A: The same multimodal deployment that reads carton photographs, sending it the written brief instead of a photograph.
options.B: The same multimodal deployment, asked to describe an existing carton in enough detail for the client to picture it.
options.C: A retrieval step over the studio's photograph library, returning the closest existing carton to the written brief.
options.D: An image generation model with the written brief, which is a different model class from the one that reads images.

rationale.correct: New images are produced by generative models from a description of what is wanted, which is a different call with a different model class from anything that reads an existing image. Image generation models are what Create new visual outputs by using generative models refers to, and the studio has no image to read because the carton has never been produced.

distractors.A: The deployment that reads cartons analyzes images that exist. Feeding it a brief asks a reading capability to produce a picture.
distractors.B: A detailed description of an existing carton is prose about the wrong carton. The client asked to see a design that has not been made.
distractors.C: Retrieval returns the nearest thing already photographed, which is by definition not the new design the brief describes.

questions.question: A university's facilities team already produces still signage graphics from written briefs with an image model.
